title: The Trinity: One God, Three Persons
subtitle: The biblical data, the four centuries the church spent working it out, and the one live debate that remains.
triageNote: This is not a hill among hills. This is the ground. The doctrine of the Trinity is the church's confession of who God is. To deny it is to worship a different God than the one Jesus revealed. Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 did not invent the doctrine. They built a fence around it after a long century of trying to hold the biblical data together without breaking it. So the existence of the triune God, three persons sharing one undivided being, is first-order. The faith itself. There is one genuine in-house debate that runs lower. The page marks it where it comes: whether the eternal relations of Father and Son include an order of authority. That argument is real. It is recent. It runs between people who all confess the Nicene Creed. Hold the doctrine with your life. Hold that one sub-question with care.
question: The first Christians were Jews who would have died before calling anyone but the Lord their God. Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. They did not abandon that confession. And then these same monotheists prayed to Jesus. They baptized in his name. They called him Lord in the sense the Old Testament reserved for the unspeakable Name. They spoke of the Spirit as God too. They did not think they had three Gods. They did not think Father, Son, and Spirit were three masks one actor wears. So what had they seen. How can the God who is one be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each fully God, each distinct from the others. Without three Gods. Without dissolving the three into one. That question took the church almost three hundred years to answer. In words that held. The answer is not a riddle to be solved but a confession to be guarded. The words it settled on, one being in three persons, eternally begotten, of one substance, were each chosen to rule out a specific way of getting God wrong.
whyItMatters:
Everything stands on this. Not as a slogan. As a structural fact. If the Son is not fully God, then the man on the cross was a creature. A creature cannot reconcile you to God. Your salvation is a rumor. Athanasius saw this with terrible clarity in the fourth century. The whole fight over a single Greek letter was a fight over whether you are saved. If the Spirit who dwells in you is not God, then God has not actually come to live in his people. The New Testament's deepest promise is empty. The Trinity is not the church's hardest puzzle bolted onto an otherwise simple faith. It is the shape of the gospel. God the Father sends God the Son in the power of God the Spirit to bring you into the life the three have always shared.

It also decides who God is in himself, before you and apart from your need of him. A solitary God is power and will. Love only arrives in such a God when there is finally something outside him to love. That makes love an afterthought and creation a kind of necessity. But the God who is Father, Son, and Spirit was love before there was a universe. The three have loved one another from eternity. God did not become loving when he made you. He is love, in himself, eternally. Your being loved is the overflow of a love that did not need you to exist in order to be real. That is not a doctrine you admire from a distance. That is the floor under every word the New Testament says about grace.

And it shapes how you pray, whether you have ever thought about it or not. You come to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. The Christian does not pray into the dark and hope. The Christian prays inside a conversation that was going on long before the world began. Carried by the Spirit. Presented by the Son. Heard by the Father. Lose the Trinity and prayer becomes a transaction with a single distant sovereign. Keep it and prayer becomes what it is, a creature drawn up into the life of God.

positions.name: Pro-Nicene orthodoxy: equal in being, ordered in relation
positions.inOneLine: Father, Son, and Spirit are one in being and equal in every divine attribute, distinguished only by their eternal relations of origin. Nothing else divides them. The order among them is an order of relation, not of authority.
positions.bestCase:
Let me give you the doctrine the church actually settled on. Everything else on this page is a footnote to it. There is one God. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each that one God, fully and without remainder. They share one indivisible divine being. They are not three parts of God. They are not three Gods. The word the council chose, homoousios, of the same substance, was chosen against a man named Arius. He taught that the Son was the highest creature, made by God before time but still made. The whole council hinged on a single letter: whether the Son is homoousios, of the same being as the Father, or homoiousios, of a similar being. Athanasius spent his life and was exiled five times over that letter. He saw that a Son who is merely similar to God is not God. And a savior who is not God cannot save.

Now, how are the three distinct if they share one undivided being. Not by being different in essence, for there is only one essence. Not by dividing up the divine attributes, for each possesses them all. They are distinguished only by their relations of origin. The Father is unbegotten. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father. The creed is careful to call this begotten, not made, lest you imagine a beginning. The Spirit eternally proceeds. These are the eternal processions, and they are the only difference among the persons. The Cappadocian fathers, Basil and the two Gregories, gave us the grammar: one ousia, one being, in three hypostases, three persons. Everything the three do toward the world they do together, because they are one God. The works of the Trinity outward are undivided. Yet each acts in the manner of his relation. The Father as source. The Son as the one through whom. The Spirit as the one in whom.

Is there an order, a taxis, among them. Yes, and the tradition has always said so. The Father is the unoriginate source, the fountainhead of deity. But hear what kind of order this is. It is an order of origin and relation, not of rank or command. The Son is begotten of the Father, so the Father is first in order. But the Son is in no way less in being, less in glory, less in authority. To be eternally from another is not to be eternally under another. The Athanasian Creed does not flinch: in this Trinity none is before or after, none is greater or less, but the whole three persons are coeternal together and coequal. So when Scripture shows the Son obeying the Father, sent by the Father, doing the Father's will, I read that as the Son's mission in the world. His taking flesh to save us. The economy of redemption. Not a window into an eternal chain of command inside God. The Son obeys in his humanity, in the days of his flesh, because he has come to do for us what we could not do. Pull that obedience back into eternity. Make the Son eternally subordinate in authority to the Father. You have quietly let Arius back in the side door. A person eternally under another's authority is not equal in deity, whatever you say with your mouth.

This is the faith of Nicaea and Constantinople, the faith confessed by the whole church, East and West, for sixteen centuries. Guard it at the center and you will not go far wrong at the edges.
advocates: the Cappadocian fathers (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa)
the framers of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
modern pro-Nicene retrieval (Lewis Ayres, Khaled Anatolios)

positions.name: Eternal functional subordination of the Son
positions.inOneLine: The Son is fully and equally God in his being. Yet from eternity, not only in the incarnation, he relates to the Father in a role of glad submission. That difference of authority and role does not touch his equality of essence.
positions.bestCase:
Let me be clear about what I am not saying, because I am routinely misheard. I am not Arius. I affirm with my whole heart that the Son is homoousios, of one being with the Father, fully God, eternal, uncreated, equal in deity and worthy of all worship. I sign the Nicene Creed without crossing my fingers. What I am asking is a narrower question. Within that perfect equality of being, is there an eternal order of relationship in which the Son joyfully submits to the Father. An order of authority, not merely of origin.

I think Scripture shows exactly this, and shows it reaching beyond the incarnation. The Son is sent by the Father, never the reverse. Sending implies authority in the one who sends. The Father is the head of Christ, Paul says, in the same breath as he names Christ the head of man. Headship in Paul is a relation of authority that does not make the one under it less in worth. Look at how the New Testament names the persons: always Father and Son, never the reverse order. A son who eternally submits to a father is honoring him, not confessing inferiority. And then there is the end of all things. After the resurrection. After the kingdom is delivered up. When there is no more curse and no more incarnate work to finish. Even then, Paul says, the Son himself will be subjected to the Father, that God may be all in all. If the Son's submission were only a temporary arrangement for the days of his flesh, why does it appear at the very consummation. By then the flesh has done its saving work. I take that as a glimpse of an order that was always there.

Why does this matter to me, and not as theological hair-splitting. Because it shows that authority and submission are not the unhappy results of the fall. They are written into the eternal life of God himself, in the most beautiful possible form. A Son who delights to do the will of a Father who loves him perfectly. Submission, in God, is not humiliation. It is glory. The Son's eternal yes to the Father is the pattern for every glad submission in the creation that images God. I hold this, with Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware, precisely to honor the Son, whose obedience the Father crowns. And to ground the goodness of order in the very being of God rather than in the wreckage of Eden.

I know the danger my friends warn of. They say an eternal subordination of authority cannot finally be kept apart from a subordination of being. That authority tracks nature. That I am letting Arius in the back door. I deny it. A human son under his father's authority for a season is fully as human as the father. Authority and equality of nature are not the same axis. I grant that the burden is on me to keep them apart. And I labor to keep them apart, because I will not surrender one inch of the Son's full deity. But I will not flatten the relations of Father and Son into a bare order of origin with no content. Not when Scripture keeps showing me a Son who, in the very form of God, did not count equality a thing to be grasped, but submitted.
advocates: much of recent complementarian evangelical theology

positions.name: Pro-Nicene equality against eternal subordination
positions.inOneLine: The Son's obedience belongs wholly to his incarnate mission, the economy of salvation. Reading an eternal hierarchy of authority back into the immanent life of God divides what cannot be divided. It threatens the Son's full deity.
positions.bestCase:
I share everything my brother across the table affirms about the Son's full deity. We are not arguing about whether the Son is God. We are arguing about whether there is an eternal hierarchy of authority inside the one God. And here I have to say, as gently as I can, that the tradition spent four centuries learning to say no to exactly this. I think it was right.

Start with what the persons share. There is one divine being, one will, one power, one authority, because there is one God. Will and authority are properties of the divine nature, not of the persons taken separately. The three persons possess the one nature wholly and equally. So to say the Son is eternally under the Father's authority is to say there are two wills in God. One commanding and one obeying. That is not Nicene Trinitarianism. That is two beings, however much you protest that you mean one. This is why the church always located the difference among the persons in the relations of origin alone, begotten and proceeding. And nowhere else. Add authority and submission as a second axis of difference and you have made the persons differ in something other than relation of origin. The tradition forbade that, precisely because that road ends at Arius. My brother says he is not Arius, and I believe his intent entirely. I am saying the logic of his position, eternal subordination of authority, cannot in the end be kept from becoming subordination of being. Authority is not a personal property floating free of nature. It tracks nature. A will that is eternally under command is a lesser will.

What then of the sending, the obedience, the Father as head, the Son subjected at the end. I read all of it as the economy, God's saving work in history, not the immanent Trinity, God as he is in himself. The Son obeys because he has become man to save us. He is sent because the work of redemption has a shape. His is the role of the one who comes. The great pro-Nicene rule goes back to Augustine and the Cappadocians. Texts which show the Son as less than the Father refer to the form of a servant he took, not the form of God in which he eternally is. Philippians says it in one sentence: being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant. The obedience is the servant form. And the subjection at the end, in First Corinthians fifteen, is the incarnate Son presenting the completed kingdom. The last act of the mediator, not a report on eternity.

Why do I press this so hard, when we agree the Son is God. Because the equality of the persons is not a side issue. It is the whole achievement of Nicaea, and it took the blood of confessors to win. And because the moment you make eternal authority and submission part of who God is, you will find people reaching for it to justify human hierarchies as divinely eternal. The deity of the Son has been made to serve an argument it was never meant to carry. Keep the Son's obedience where Scripture and the creeds put it, in his mission for us. Then the Son stands exactly as high as the Father, which is to say, no order of command runs through the eternal God at all.
advocates: the historic pro-Nicene consensus (Augustine, the Cappadocians)
much of confessional Reformed and catholic theology

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The deity of the Son, claimed by all orthodox views
biblicalEvidence.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Two claims held together in one sentence: the Word is distinct from God, with God, and the Word is God. John then says all things were made through him. That places the Word on the Creator's side of the line between Creator and creature.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Decisive against Arianism and any view that makes the Son a creature, since what is made through the Word cannot itself be made.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three positions on this page affirm it fully. The pro-Nicene reading stresses that with God and was God together require both real distinction and full deity. That is the whole grammar of the doctrine. Those who hold eternal functional subordination note that the Word is named in relation, with God, and take that relation to carry an eternal order. Their critics answer that the relation here is one of origin and intimacy, not authority.

biblicalEvidence.summary: I and the Father are one. Spoken in a dispute over whether the Son's works are the Father's works. The crowd takes up stones because they hear a man making himself God. The oneness is strong enough to provoke a charge of blasphemy.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that wants a real gap of rank between Father and Son. The unity here is so close it sounds, to the hearers, like a claim to deity.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Pro-Nicene readers take one as a unity of being and power. Subordinationists note the neuter form, one thing rather than one person. They read it as unity of purpose and work rather than a denial of relational order, while still affirming full deity. Both agree it rules out the Son being a mere creature.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The triune name, claimed by all
biblicalEvidence.summary: Baptizing them in the name, singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. One name, three persons. The risen Jesus places the three together as the single object of the church's baptismal allegiance. It is the closest the Gospels come to a formula.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for modalism, which would make the three mere modes, since baptism is into the name of all three as distinct. And hard for tritheism. The name is one.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All orthodox views read this as the seed of the doctrine: one divine name, three distinct persons. The order Father, Son, Spirit is noted by subordinationists as a fixed taxis. Pro-Nicenes answer that an order of naming reflects the relations of origin, the Father as source. It need not imply an order of authority.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested between the two readings of order
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Jews sought to kill him because he called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then Jesus answers that the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. Equality with God and dependence on the Father, in adjacent verses.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any flat account: verse 18 gives full equality, verse 19 gives the Son doing only what he sees the Father do. The passage refuses to let you drop either.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Eternal functional subordination reads verse 19 as the Son's eternal posture of acting from and after the Father. An order that runs deeper than the incarnation. Pro-Nicene equality reads the Son can do nothing of his own accord as the inseparable operations of the one God. The Son never acts apart from the Father because they are one being. And it reads any subordinate cast as the form of a servant assumed for our salvation. Both insist on verse 18's equality.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God. The relation of God to Christ is set alongside relations of headship. In Paul those carry the sense of authority.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against pro-Nicene equality, since it names God as the head of Christ in a chain of headship relations. It seems to set an order of authority between Father and Son.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Subordinationists take this as authority within equality, the same pattern they see in the Son's eternal relation to the Father. Pro-Nicene readers answer in two ways. First, head, kephale, can carry the sense of source rather than ruler, the head as the spring from which something flows. Second, the Father is here the head of the incarnate Christ, the mediator, the one who took the form of a servant. Not a statement about the eternal Son apart from his mission.

biblicalEvidence.summary: When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all. The Son's subjection appears at the very end, after the kingdom is delivered up.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the view that the Son's subjection is only a temporary feature of the incarnation. It appears at the consummation. And hard for any view that makes the subjection define the Son's eternal being. It is framed as the climax of a saving work that has an end.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Eternal functional subordination reads the Son's subjection at the end as the unveiling of an order that was always there. Pro-Nicene readers take it as the final act of the mediator. The incarnate Son, having completed the kingdom, presents it and himself as man to the Father, so that God is all in all. That is the close of the economy of redemption, not a description of the immanent Trinity. The phrase God may be all in all is read by pro-Nicenes as the goal of redemption. Not the imposition of rank within God.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Pro-Nicene equality, with subordinationists drawing on it
biblicalEvidence.summary: Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The form of God and the form of a servant are set in deliberate contrast. The obedience to death belongs to the servant form he assumed.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for eternal functional subordination as a reading of the Son's eternal life. It locates the obedience precisely in the form of a servant he took, not in the form of God he eternally had.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Pro-Nicene readers treat this as the master text for the rule that humbling and obedience belong to the assumed servant form, the economy. Equality belongs to the form of God. Subordinationists answer that one who did not grasp at equality but submitted shows a disposition of glad deference. They take that deference to be eternal, not invented at the incarnation, though they grant the deepest humbling is the servant's.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The deity of the Son, claimed by all orthodox views
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Son is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. The Son shares the very nature of God and does the work only God can do, sustaining all things.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Decisive against any subordination of being, since the Son is the exact imprint of God's very nature and upholds creation, a divine work.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All orthodox views affirm it as a high statement of the Son's full deity. Pro-Nicenes note that radiance and imprint language gives distinction without division. The radiance is not less than the light. The verse is common ground. The debate over authority is fought elsewhere, since here only nature and divine work are in view.

weighing:
My judgment, offered as one pastor thinking out loud, not as a verdict you must accept to be orthodox.

First, the thing that is not up for debate. The doctrine of the Trinity itself, one God in three persons, the Son and Spirit fully and equally God, is the faith. I hold it without hesitation and without the sense that I am holding a private opinion. Nicaea and Constantinople were not committees overreaching. They were the church learning, under pressure, to say what the New Testament had already shown. The God of Israel is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Athanasius was right. The cost he paid to be right is part of why I can write this sentence at all. If you take nothing else from this page, take that the Trinity is not negotiable and not a puzzle bolted onto the gospel. It is the gospel's own shape.

Now the one live debate. On whether the Son is eternally subordinate in authority to the Father, I find myself with the pro-Nicene equality reading. I will tell you why, tentatively. The decisive point for me is the unity of will. If there is one divine being, there is one divine will. A Son eternally under the Father's authority introduces a second will into God, one that commands and one that obeys. The tradition saw that. It located the difference among the persons only in the relations of origin, begotten and proceeding. The point was precise: nothing in the divine nature, including authority, would be divided among them. When I read the obedience texts, the sending, the head of Christ is God, the subjection at the end, they read most naturally to me as the economy. The Son's saving mission. The form of a servant. And Philippians two seems to say so almost in as many words. I also notice, and this gives me pause about the other view, that an eternal hierarchy inside God is hard to keep from sliding into a hierarchy of being. However firmly its defenders deny that they mean it.

But I want to say two honest things on the other side. The men who hold eternal functional subordination, Grudem and Ware among them, are not Arians. They do not deserve to be called such. They affirm the full deity of the Son as loudly as anyone. And they are reaching for something true. The relations of Father and Son are not interchangeable. Order and glad deference can be beautiful rather than degrading. And they have real texts, especially the Son's subjection at the very end in First Corinthians fifteen. That one is genuinely harder for my position than I would like. So I land here: the Trinity, first-order, settled, the floor. The eternal-authority question, a real debate among the orthodox. I lean firmly pro-Nicene there, while granting it is an argument inside the family and not a wall between believers.
charitableDisagreement:
Be careful how you fight this one. Two very different things are on the table, and treating them the same does damage in both directions. The doctrine of the Trinity is first-order. Someone who denies that the Son is fully God, who makes him a creature or a mode, has stepped outside the Christian confession. Clarity there is not unkindness. It is the most basic honesty the church owes. Arius was not a brother with an interesting alternative. He was wrong about who God is. The church was right to say so plainly.

The debate over eternal authority and submission is a different kind of thing. The temperature of it in recent years has not been to anyone's credit. Brothers who confess every line of the Nicene Creed have called each other heretics over it. That is a scandal. If you hold the pro-Nicene equality view, as I lean to, do not call those who hold eternal functional subordination Arians. They are not. And the accusation tells more about your zeal than your accuracy. If you hold eternal functional subordination, do not treat the pro-Nicene insistence on one will and one authority as a cold abstraction. It does not empty the Father-Son relation of all content. It is the hard-won grammar that kept the Son fully God.

So, is it a hill to die on. The Trinity, yes, with everything you have. To lose it is to lose the God of the gospel. The eternal-authority question, no. It is a debate the church can hold, and hold better than it has lately, between people who kneel before the same triune God. Defend the doctrine like the ground it is. Conduct the sub-debate like a family argument among people who will spend eternity together in the presence of the God they are arguing about.

relatedDebates.topic: The filioque and the procession of the Spirit
relatedDebates.note: The original Constantinopolitan creed says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Western church later added and the Son, the filioque. The Eastern church never accepted it, and it remains a central difference between East and West. The question is whether the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son together. It bears directly on how the three persons are ordered.

relatedDebates.topic: Modalism, Arianism, and the boundaries the creeds drew
relatedDebates.note: The doctrine was hammered out against two opposite errors. Modalism, that Father, Son, and Spirit are three masks of one person, collapses the three. Arianism, that the Son is the highest creature, collapses the deity. Every phrase of the Nicene Creed is aimed at one or the other. That is why the wording matters and cannot be loosened without letting an old error back in.

relatedDebates.topic: The eternal generation of the Son
relatedDebates.note: The creed calls the Son begotten, not made, eternally begotten of the Father. Some recent evangelicals questioned whether eternal generation is biblical or merely a Greek philosophical import. Others have argued strongly for its recovery. Where you stand shapes how you understand what distinguishes the persons at all. The relations of origin are the only difference the tradition allows.
